As of 256 PM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Our weather system has arrived in portions of 
northern New York at the time of this discussion, with radar 
denoting areas of stratiform rain showers across the Adirondacks
and St. Lawrence Valley. Isentropic lift along a warm front 
will continue to spread east this afternoon with light to 
moderate stratiform rain moving into central and northern 
Vermont. Stratiform rain will become more broken and scattery by
this evening as a strong low level jet of 40- 50kts at 850mb 
builds in. While most of these stronger winds aloft will not be 
realized due to concurrent precipitation, gusts between 25-35 
MPH will be possible, especially in the favored south-north 
channeled valleys. For mariners, a Lake Wind Advisory is in 
effect for Lake Champlain through at least tomorrow morning. The
low-level jet will be associated with a small warm sector ahead
of a clearing cold front which will help transition showers 
around sunset to more convective driven showers. Instability 
will be elevated and not surface based, and likely will be 
competing with the preceding stable air from todays stratiform 
rain. That said, a few isolated rumbles of thunder, primarily in
the St. Lawrence Valley and Adirondacks will be possible with 
just under 500J/kg of elevated MLCAPE analyzed currently, and 
subsequent strong 40-50knots of shear. No severe or strong 
storms are expected, however.

While the system will be fairly progressive, Pwats in the 
latest CAMs denote elevated values to around 1.8-2.25 inches 
areawide with warm cloud depths to 12,000ft agl. As rain turns 
more showery towards later this afternoon and evening, heavy 
downpours will be possible. Rain should be beneficial with the 
recent dry stretch and antecedent dry conditions through this 
summer, thus no hydrological concerns are anticipated with this 
system. Precipitation amounts will be highest across the St. 
Lawrence Valley, higher terrain of the Adirondacks and spine of 
the Greens, and near the International Border. Recent CAMs have 
begun to trend some higher rainfall amounts a bit south into 
central Vermont. While these are likely contaminated with more 
robust convection that appears unlikely, this trend south has 
been reflected in the latest QPF forecast, where rainfall 
amounts along a line from Tupper Lake, NY to eastern Addison 
have been slightly increased. Some shadowing and less robust 
convection will help to reduce the magnitude models are 
suggesting. Blocked flow with low Froude numbers will also 
likely lead to some orographic enhancement of precipitation 
totals along the spine of the Greens. Around three-quarters of 
an inch to and inch of rain will be possible in the 
aforementioned locations, with a quarter to half an inch most 
other locations; lower amounts likely in southeastern Vermont, 
and in portions of the central Champlain Valley due to shadowing
from the Adirondacks. Temperatures tonight will be mild in the 
mid 60s with precipitation and humid conditions ongoing. Rain 
showers will taper off towards sunrise Thursday morning, with 
slightly weakening winds.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Our dynamic weather system today will slide east
Thursday morning with drier low level conditions mixing in from
the north and west. Mid level moisture will linger into 
Thursday afternoon with some clearing conditions, mainly in the 
wider valley; the higher terrain will likely remain partly to 
mostly cloudy tomorrow. Temperatures will be warmer than today 
with mixing and highs in the mid to upper 70s. Winds will become
gusty once again Thursday afternoon with good vertical mixing 
associated with a lagging low level jet, and drying low levels 
behind the Wednesday system. Winds will gust between 20-30 MPH, 
primarily in the channeled north to south valleys of the Vermont
and New York. Winds will trend weaker by late Thursday with 
calmer northwest cold advection by Friday. Depending on how fast
winds slacken Thursday evening, and how fast drier low levels 
will advect, some patchy fog, mainly in the Adirondacks, and 
perhaps the St. Lawrence Valley, will be possible, as skies will
begin to clear overnight from west to east. Vermont will likely
lag behind in the clearing department with clouds lingering 
towards sunrise Friday. Thursday night lows will dip into the 
40s for most of the region, outside of areas near Lake 
Champlain. The Adirondacks have the best opportunity to radiate 
out with some pocket upper 30s in the typical coldest hollows.

A picture perfect weekend looks to be in store, beginning 
Friday through Saturday. Temperatures will trend slightly below 
seasonable levels Friday as northwest flow advects cooler air 
from Canada. Highs will be in the mid 60s to near 70 with clear 
skies. A few light breezes near the International Border, and 
Champlain Valley, to 10-15 MPH could bring a slight bite to the 
air Friday afternoon. Clear skies will persist Friday night with
